meta.task_prompt:
Implement GitHub issue #9 on this repo: "add redis caching in auth proxy for kanban endpoints."

There is already a shared Redis client at `internal/pkg/redis/main.go`, and it is
already used elsewhere in the codebase (see `internal/app/server.go` and
`internal/pkg/server/permissions/perm.go` for the existing usage pattern). Follow
that same pattern rather than inventing a new one.

Scope:
- Add caching for the read paths in `internal/pkg/server/routes/kanban.go`.
- Add cache invalidation on the corresponding write paths, so a write never
  leaves a stale cached read behind.
- Pick sane key naming and TTLs consistent with how the existing Redis usage in
  this repo does it.
- This repo currently has no test files. Do not feel obligated to introduce a
  whole test framework for this change, but do double check the code compiles
  and, if there's an easy way to sanity-check the caching behavior manually
  (e.g. a local run), do that.

When you are done, close with a single clear paragraph summarizing exactly what
you changed and why — that summary becomes the pull request's title and body
verbatim, so make it read like a real PR description, not an internal note.

code_review.summary: The PR adds read-through caching to the four kanban GET handlers that had none (GetLabel, getItem, exportKanban, getKanban). For the three JSON endpoints it copies the existing GetLabels/getItems pattern closely: GetItemFromRedis, then StructToMap, then AddItemToRedis, with the same 24h TTL and the same X-cache: HIT header. It also adds exact-key invalidation on the item and comment write paths. The code compiles and is easy to read. However, it does not meet the task's hard requirement that 'a write never leaves a stale cached read behind'. kanbanProto.Item embeds `repeated Comment comments`, and GetItemResponse (the payload of the already-cached `<board>:items:page:*` keys) is a list of Items. Yet AddComment, UpdateComment and DeleteComment only delete `item:<id>`, so paginated item lists keep serving stale comments for up to 24h. The fix for the reviewer-flagged gap makes `item_id` a required query parameter on PATCH/DELETE /kanban/comment. That is a breaking API change for existing clients, and it still trusts a client-supplied id that is never checked against the comment. exportKanban now caches a `downloadLink` for 24h, which is questionable for an export artifact. Finally, the new `item:`/`label:` keys are not scoped to a board, so the repo's existing board-prefix invalidation (DeleteAllKeysPrefix) cannot cover them. That design choice is the root cause of the comment-invalidation problem.

findings.summary: Comment writes delete only `item:<id>` and leave the cached paginated item lists (`<board>:items:page:N:limit:M`) stale, even though every Item in those lists embeds its comments.
findings.failure_scenario: A client calls GET /kanban/items?page=1&limit=10, which caches `<board>:items:page:1:limit:10` with each Item's `comments` array. It then POSTs /kanban/comment?item_id=X. AddComment deletes only `item:X`. The next GET /kanban/items returns X-cache: HIT with the old comment list, and stays stale for up to 24h until an item create/update/delete happens on that board. UpdateComment and DeleteComment (lines 315, 338) have the same problem.
findings.suggested_fix: Also invalidate the board-scoped caches on comment writes, for example `redis.DeleteAllKeysPrefix(c.Request.Header.Get("X-Board"))`, and require X-Board on these routes the way createItem/updateItem already use it. Better still, key the item cache under the board (`<board>:item:<id>`) so one prefix delete covers every derived view.

findings.summary: UpdateComment and DeleteComment now return 400 unless a brand-new `item_id` query parameter is sent, which breaks existing clients, and the supplied value is trusted without any check that the comment belongs to that item.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) An existing frontend that calls PATCH /kanban/comment?comment_id=C, the only contract before this PR, now gets `400 item_id is required`, so editing and deleting comments is broken until every client is updated. The reviewer's own search (trace line 149) found no caller that sends item_id. (b) A client that sends the wrong item_id gets a 200 with the comment updated, but the real item's `item:<id>` cache is never deleted and stays stale for 24h. The same logic appears at line 333 in DeleteComment.
findings.suggested_fix: Don't make cache invalidation depend on an unverified parameter that breaks the API. Use the board-prefix invalidation described in code-1 (X-Board is already the repo's convention for board-scoped writes). Alternatively, resolve the parent item on the server once the kanban service exposes it. If item_id must stay, make it optional and fall back to the board-prefix delete when it is missing, rather than rejecting the request.

findings.summary: exportKanban now caches `ExportResponse{downloadLink}` for 24h, even though an export link usually points at a point-in-time snapshot and/or a URL that expires.
findings.failure_scenario: A user exports the board and gets link L, which is cached under `<board>:export`. They then add a label (createLabel deletes only `<board>:Labels`) or a comment (which never touches board keys) and export again. They get the cached L, which reflects the old board state. If the kanban service issues presigned or expiring links shorter than 24h, later calls return a dead link.
findings.suggested_fix: Leave the export endpoint uncached. It is a user-triggered, low-frequency action where freshness matters more than latency. If it must be cached, use a short TTL, and invalidate it on label and comment writes as well.

findings.summary: The new `item:<id>` and `label:<id>` keys use a global entity-prefix scheme, while the existing kanban keys are board-scoped (`<board>:Labels`, `<board>:items:...`), so the repo's `DeleteAllKeysPrefix(board)` invalidation cannot reach them.
findings.failure_scenario: Because item keys sit outside the board namespace, every write has to know the exact item id to invalidate it. That is how the comment handlers ended up needing a new `item_id` parameter (code-2). A future bulk board operation that only calls DeleteAllKeysPrefix(board) would silently leave `item:*` entries stale.
findings.suggested_fix: Follow the existing convention: `<board>:item:<id>` and `<board>:label:<id>`. Then the existing prefix deletes cover them, and the extra `DeleteFromRedis("item:"+...)` calls in updateItem and DeleteItem are no longer needed.

findings.summary: getKanban calls `redis.Rdb.Get` and `redis.Rdb.Set` directly with `context.Background()` and a duplicated `1*86400*time.Second` literal, bypassing the helper layer in internal/pkg/redis that the task asked the change to follow.
findings.failure_scenario: This is the only route handler that uses the raw client, and it pulls `context` and `time` into the routes package just for that. If the TTL is ever changed in AddItemToRedis, this key keeps the old TTL. The write-gate judge flagged the matching import edit with scope_creep 0.71 (trace line 95).
findings.suggested_fix: Add small string helpers next to the existing ones in internal/pkg/redis/main.go, for example `GetStringFromRedis(key) (string, bool)` and `AddStringToRedis(key, val string)`, reusing the same TTL. Call those from getKanban and drop the `context`/`time` imports from kanban.go.

findings.summary: Nothing exercises the new cache HIT/MISS or invalidation paths, and the reviewer's mutation spot-check confirmed that inverting the getKanban hit condition still passes verification.
findings.failure_scenario: At trace line 193 the reviewer mutated `if err == nil {` to `if err != nil {` in getKanban, and `go build && go vet` still passed. Regressions like the stale-comment case in code-1 would ship undetected. The task waived a test framework but asked for a manual sanity check if one was easy, and none was attempted.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a small handler test using miniredis plus httptest for at least getItem, covering miss then hit, and AddComment followed by a miss. Or document a curl-based manual check against a local redis-server in the PR description.

process_review.summary: The run finished with a compiling PR, respected read-before-edit throughout, and the first reviewer caught a real gap. It still cost $2.69 over 152 tool calls and 142 model turns across 7 subagents (about 32 minutes of wall-clock time per the trace timestamps) for a 58-line single-file change. That is disproportionate. The main cost drivers were: (1) a spurious 'placeholder' ask agent spawned at the start; (2) a coder that died on a provider error after an empty read_file call, forcing a full redo; (3) a second coder that read the evidence showing no caller sends item_id (trace lines 62, 115), knowingly shipped a no-op invalidation anyway ('unconfirmed, but per task this is acceptable', line 131), and so triggered a whole review/fix cycle; (4) a first reviewer that alone spent $0.97, 31 turns and 880s on scattershot searches (reactions, README, swagger, git_log, three separate board_id searches), during which the loop_control judge's making_progress score fell to 0.27–0.29; and (5) a second reviewer that repeated near-identical searches, hit loop_control stop_early (repeating_itself 0.69, line 299), and ended status=stopped without a verdict. After that the PR was opened anyway. Navigation mostly followed search → read_file windows, with a few places where find_symbol would have been cheaper. The build was checked with `go build` (ok at lines 120, 134, 260), but the harness verify at line 296 reported FAILED (pre-existing vet warnings), and no manual caching check was ever attempted despite the coder's claim that none was possible. The orchestrator's closing message was a bullet list with caveats, not the single PR-ready paragraph the task required, and the PR body ended up being the raw task text.

findings.summary: The orchestrator spawned a second ask agent with the literal task 'placeholder' alongside the real survey agent.
findings.evidence: Trace line 3: ask tool call with arguments {"task": "placeholder"} started agent 5cd68480. The transcript later admits 'I made an accidental duplicate spawn there — apologies'. The merge_gate at line 8 scored accomplished_its_brief at 0.26. Cost was small ($0.016), but it was pure waste.

findings.summary: The first coder issued a malformed read_file with no arguments and then failed with a provider error, leaving no diff and forcing a full restart.
findings.evidence: Line 32: read_file with {} returned 'error: read_file() missing 1 required positional argument: 'path''. The loop_control judge failed at line 31, the merge_gate at line 33 scored accomplished_its_brief at 0.04, and the transcript shows 'status: failed summary: error: Provider returned error'. The retry coder at line 35/36 found 'dirty: False' and '(no diff)'.

findings.summary: The retry coder re-ran the exact search the failed coder had already run, and re-read the same two windows of kanban.go.
findings.evidence: Line 42 search pattern 'func GetItem|func AddComment|func UpdateComment|func DeleteComment' in internal/pkg/RPC/kanban is identical to line 30 from agent 734ee6f1. Lines 38/40 re-read kanban.go 1-200 and 200-285, the same as lines 27/29. result_screen shows cache_hit: true at lines 37 and 39. This is understandable after a crash, but the continue_from handoff did not carry the findings over.

findings.summary: The coder ran overlapping searches for the comment routes and item_id three or more times.
findings.evidence: Line 53 search 'Comment' in internal/pkg/server/routes, line 59 'comment' in routes/main.go, line 65 '/kanban/comment' repo-wide: all returned the same main.go:46-48 lines. item_id was searched repo-wide at line 62, again at line 107 (in kanban.go) and at line 115 ('comment_id|item_id' in internal). Struct lookups in the 2093-line kanban.pb.go (lines 45, 49, 55, 60) used search followed by a read_file window where find_symbol would have returned the definition and its position in one call.

findings.summary: The coder had evidence that no caller sends item_id to PATCH/DELETE /kanban/comment but shipped a silently no-op invalidation anyway, which caused a full extra review and fix cycle.
findings.evidence: Reasoning at lines 131/134: 'UpdateComment and DeleteComment routes don't accept an `item_id` query param in existing frontend calls (unconfirmed), but per task this is acceptable since it's "whatever item-id-bearing param is available"'. The earlier search at line 115 ('comment_id|item_id') had shown only the AddComment usage. Reviewer 6e130169 then returned 'request changes' on exactly this point, which led to coder 298aacdc and reviewer 15e114e3.

findings.summary: The coder said a local caching sanity check was not possible ('no docker/redis-server confirmed running') without ever running a command to check.
findings.evidence: The only run_command calls in the whole trace are line 120 'go build ./... 2>&1 | head -50', line 134 'go build ./... ... && go vet ./internal/pkg/server/routes/...' and line 260 'go build ./... 2>&1', all exit 0. No `which redis-server`, `docker ps` or similar was attempted, yet the coder's summary claims 'No live Redis/gRPC backend available in this environment'. go vet was run only on the routes package, and the harness's full `go build ./... && go vet ./...` at line 296 reported 'verdict: FAILED' (pre-existing copylocks).

findings.summary: The write_gate judge flagged the edit adding the context/time imports (needed only for getKanban's hand-rolled Redis calls) with an elevated scope_creep score. It was not enforced and the run did not react.
findings.evidence: Line 95 write_gate response: scope_creep score 0.71 (confidence 0.51). The edit at line 97 added "context" and "time" imports. stats.json shows 12 write_gate 'flag' outcomes, all enforced: false. The coder did not revisit the design, and the getKanban deviation from the helper pattern shipped (see code-5).

findings.summary: The first reviewer was the most expensive agent in the run ($0.97, 31 turns, 880s, over a third of total cost) and spent much of that on scattershot, repeated searches unrelated to a 60-line diff.
findings.evidence: It searched for reactions three times (lines 184, 187, 188), board_id three times (164, 194, 210), '/kanban/comment' twice (158, 166), plus README 'redis|cache' (200), 'swagger|openapi|api.md|docs/' (204), git_log (201), list_files (172) and todo_scan (197). The loop_control judge at line 196 scored making_progress 0.27 and repeating_itself 0.52, and at line 203 making_progress 0.29. The substantive finding (item_id gap) was already visible from the diff plus the item_id search at line 149.

findings.summary: The re-review reviewer repeated near-identical searches and was stopped early by loop_control, ending status=stopped without a verdict.
findings.evidence: Lines 275 and 277 search 'StatusBadRequest' and then 'c\.String\(http\.StatusBadRequest', which returned identical results. Line 272 re-read redis/main.go and lines 283/286 ran git_log twice. The loop_control judge at line 299 scored making_progress 0.21 and repeating_itself 0.69 (the single stop_early decision in stats.json). The merge_gate at line 300 scored accomplished_its_brief at 0.06. The transcript shows 'status: stopped ... did not read the live file contents or diff' (in fact it had, at lines 268/270/280).

findings.summary: After the stopped review, the orchestrator visibly second-guessed its own policy mid-message and asked the user whether to re-review, but the PR was opened seconds later without an independent verdict. Its closing message was not the single-paragraph PR description the task required.
findings.evidence: Transcript 02:47:02: 'I'll respawn a reviewer once ... per policy (stopped → don't respawn automatically... actually let me reconsider: policy says if status=stopped, tell the user, don't respawn)'. At 02:47:09: 'opened pull request ... /pull/17'. The final message is a bullet list with a caveat paragraph. The PR body in pr.md is the raw task text ('A/B side: reach-auth-proxy\n\nTask: ...') and the title is the truncated task, not a written summary.

findings.summary: The fix coder re-read files whose relevant content it had just pulled with search, and re-read redis/main.go after finishing its edits.
findings.evidence: Line 234 searched 'comment|Comment' in routes/main.go and line 239 then read all of routes/main.go. Line 235 searched the redis helper signatures, but line 255 still read all of redis/main.go (result_screen cache_hit: true at line 254) after both str_replace edits (245, 253) were done. Line 230 re-read all of kanban.proto, which the prior reviewer had already summarised in the task handoff.

strengths: The JSON endpoints closely follow the existing GetLabels/getItems caching pattern: GetItemFromRedis/AddItemToRedis, a 24h TTL, and the X-cache: HIT header.
The change is confined to kanban.go, compiles cleanly, and introduces no new vet warnings.
The coder correctly found that Item embeds Comments and added item-cache invalidation to the comment handlers.
The first reviewer caught a real correctness gap, and the orchestrator routed it back for a fix.
There were no read-before-edit violations, and every edit was preceded by a read of kanban.go.
concerns: Comment writes still leave the cached `<board>:items:page:*` lists stale for up to 24h, so the task's hard requirement is not met.
Requiring `item_id` on PATCH/DELETE /kanban/comment is an unannounced breaking API change, and the value is trusted without checking it against the comment.
A 24h cache on an export download link is likely wrong.
The final re-review was stopped by loop_control, and the PR shipped without an independent verdict on the fix.
Spend was about $2.69, 152 tool calls and 7 agents for a 58-line single-file diff, with the first reviewer alone using over a third of it.
The PR body is the raw task text rather than the requested one-paragraph description, and no manual caching check was attempted.
overall_assessment.narrative: The diff is a reasonable first pass that copies the repo's caching idiom, but it inherits a design flaw: item and label keys sit outside the board namespace. That flaw drove most of the run's churn. The coder knowingly left a no-op invalidation in place, a reviewer caught it, and the fix swapped a silent bug for a breaking 400 on the comment endpoints. Meanwhile the more pervasive staleness in the cached item lists went unnoticed by both reviewers. On the process side, the navigation and edit discipline were fine, but the run paid for a placeholder agent, a crashed coder, an unfocused $0.97 review, and a looping re-review that ended without a verdict before the PR was opened. Board-scoping the new keys and invalidating by board prefix on comment writes would fix the correctness issues and remove the need for the item_id parameter.
